res.cls: Piastri and Hülkenberg did not start; Alonso, Bottas and Hadjar retired.
18 classified; Hülkenberg, Lawson, Gasly and Hadjar retired.
16 classified, 5 retirements; Lindblad did not start.
14 classified, 8 not classified. Hamilton's first win for Ferrari.
18 classified; Stroll, Sainz, Pérez and Bottas retired.
Top three covered by 0.772s. Verstappen, Albon and Hülkenberg retired.
19 classified; Stroll, Pérez and Russell retired.
19 classified; Piastri, Pérez and Bottas retired.
Antonelli won from 19th on the grid after a power unit penalty, the first Italian to win at Monza since 1966. Leclerc crashed on lap 2, bringing a red flag.
First race at the new Madrid street circuit. Sainz, Pérez, Stroll and Hamilton retired.
Held on a Saturday. Russell held Verstappen off by 0.196s; 7 retirements.
Moved from April and relocated to Sepang, F1's first visit to Malaysia in nine years. Verstappen's first win of 2026, from pole.

Verstappen converted pole into his first Singapore win, completing a Sprint and Grand Prix double: he squeezed Leclerc at Turn 1 and kept the lead through his only stop. Leclerc took second by passing Hamilton on lap 46, and Antonelli climbed to third late on, passing Norris and Hamilton, while Hamilton, who had switched to softs early, faded to sixth. Russell recovered from 19th on the grid to ninth. Antonelli now leads Russell by 102 points and can clinch the title in Austin.

2025.sum: McLaren had the fastest car for most of the year and Oscar Piastri led the standings through the summer. Verstappen mounted a late charge in a slower Red Bull, turning it into a three-way fight that went to Abu Dhabi, where Norris took his first title by two points.
keys: McLaren clinched the constructors' title with six rounds to spare.
Hamilton's first season at Ferrari ended without a Grand Prix win.
Final year of the 2022–2025 ground-effect rules.

2024.sum: Verstappen won seven of the first ten races, then Red Bull lost its edge as McLaren upgraded its car. Norris took his first win in Miami, but Verstappen's consistency and a drive from 17th to win in wet Brazil secured a fourth straight title.
keys: McLaren won its first constructors' title since 1998.
A record 24-race calendar.
Seven different drivers won races.

2023.sum: The most dominant season in F1 history. Red Bull won 21 of 22 Grands Prix, with Carlos Sainz's Singapore victory the only exception, and Verstappen set records for wins in a season and consecutive wins.
keys: Verstappen won 10 races in a row.
Las Vegas returned to the calendar on the Strip.
Sprint format expanded to six weekends.

2022.sum: Ground-effect rules arrived and Ferrari started strongest, with Leclerc winning two of the first three races. Reliability failures and strategy errors let Red Bull take over, and Verstappen clinched his second title in Japan.
keys: First year of the ground-effect regulations.
Miami joined the calendar.
Mercedes won only one race, in Brazil.

2021.sum: Verstappen and Hamilton fought all year, with collisions at Silverstone and Monza. They arrived in Abu Dhabi level on points, and a disputed safety car restart on the final lap gave Verstappen his first title.
keys: Mercedes won an eighth straight constructors' title.
Sprint qualifying debuted at Silverstone.
Race director Michael Masi was replaced after the finale.

2020.sum: The pandemic delayed the start until July in Austria, with a reshaped 17-race calendar that brought back Imola, Portimão, Mugello and the Nürburgring. Hamilton won his seventh title, equalling Michael Schumacher's record.
keys: Pierre Gasly won at Monza for AlphaTauri.
Sergio Pérez took his first win in Sakhir.
Romain Grosjean escaped a fiery crash in Bahrain.

16.wxnote: Race started on a wet track; leaders switched from intermediates to slicks under the lap-9 safety car.

17.wxnote: Dry race on slicks throughout. Torrential rain delayed Saturday's Sprint, which started on intermediates from a standing start after two formation laps behind the safety car.

GRIDNOTES.1: Stroll, Sainz and Verstappen were allowed to start after not setting a time within 107% of the fastest Q1 lap.
GRIDNOTES.2: Albon was sent to the pit lane after his car was modified under parc fermé conditions; he then did not start.
GRIDNOTES.4: Hadjar was disqualified from qualifying but allowed to race, starting from the pit lane after taking extra power unit elements.
GRIDNOTES.5: Stroll started from the pit lane after his car was modified under parc fermé conditions, including new power unit elements.
GRIDNOTES.7: Alonso started from the pit lane after his car was modified under parc fermé conditions.
GRIDNOTES.9: Gasly: 3-place penalty for impeding in qualifying. Stroll: 10-place penalty for extra power unit elements.
GRIDNOTES.10: Alonso (20 places) and Hadjar (30 places) sent to the back of the grid. Stroll, Sainz and Norris: 10-place penalties for extra power unit elements.
GRIDNOTES.11: Hamilton: 3-place penalty for impeding in qualifying. Antonelli: 3-place penalty for not slowing for yellow flags. Pérez started from the pit lane (parc fermé changes).
GRIDNOTES.12: Pérez started from the pit lane after his car was modified under parc fermé conditions.
GRIDNOTES.13: Antonelli and Albon sent to the back of the grid for extra power unit elements. Piastri: 3-place penalty for impeding. Alonso and Lawson started from the pit lane (power unit elements).
GRIDNOTES.14: Bearman and Stroll were allowed to race without a qualifying time. Stroll: 40-place power unit penalty. Sainz: 3-place penalty for impeding. Bearman started from the pit lane (parc fermé changes).
GRIDNOTES.15: Alonso (30 places) and Stroll (20 places): power unit penalties. Sainz: 5 places for not slowing for yellow flags. Pérez: 3 places for impeding.
GRIDNOTES.16: Colapinto: 5 places for causing a collision at the previous round plus 10 for power unit elements. Lindblad: 30 places and Hadjar: 5 places for power unit elements.
GRIDNOTES.17: Russell starts from the back after a 40-place grid penalty for using additional power unit elements. Alonso starts from the pit lane after Aston Martin changed his turbocharger under parc fermé. Stroll starts from the pit lane for a parc fermé breach, as his car was still uncovered in the garage after the post-qualifying time limit. Hadjar starts from the pit lane after Red Bull changed his engine, exhaust and turbocharger; he had set no time in qualifying.

McLaren.name: McLaren
McLaren.stats_basis: McLaren constructor record, 1966 Monaco GP to 2025 Abu Dhabi GP (entries 998; starts 994)
McLaren.history: Founded by New Zealander Bruce McLaren in 1963, the team made its Grand Prix debut at Monaco in 1966 and took its first win in 1968. It became one of the sport's great powers through the Fittipaldi/Hunt, Prost/Lauda, Senna/Prost and Häkkinen eras, and is the second-most successful team after Ferrari. After a lean spell in the 2010s it returned to the top under Zak Brown and Andrea Stella, winning back-to-back constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025.
highlights: 10 Constructors' and 13 Drivers' Championships
Back-to-back Constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, plus Lando Norris's 2025 Drivers' title
Senna/Prost MP4/4 won 15 of 16 races in 1988
Only constructor to have won the Triple Crown of Motorsport (Monaco GP, Indy 500, Le Mans)

Mercedes.name: Mercedes
Mercedes.founder: Daimler-Benz (modern team from the 2009 purchase of Brawn GP)
Mercedes.stats_basis: Mercedes constructor record, 1954–1955 and 2010–2025 (excludes Tyrrell/BAR/Honda/Brawn predecessors)
Mercedes.history: Mercedes-Benz first raced in the World Championship in 1954–55, when Juan Manuel Fangio won two titles before the factory withdrew. The modern Brackley team descends from Tyrrell, which became British American Racing (1999), Honda (2006) and the title-winning Brawn GP (2009) before Daimler took it over and raced it as Mercedes from 2010. It went on to dominate the V6 turbo-hybrid era.
highlights: Record eight consecutive Constructors' Championships (2014–2021)
Seven consecutive Drivers' Championships 2014–2020 (Hamilton six, Rosberg one)
Fangio won the 1954 and 1955 Drivers' titles
Nine Drivers' Championships in total

Red Bull Racing.name: Red Bull Racing
Red Bull Racing.stats_basis: Red Bull Racing constructor record, 2005–2025 (excludes Stewart and Jaguar)
Red Bull Racing.history: Red Bull bought the Jaguar Racing team, itself the former Stewart Grand Prix outfit founded in 1997, in November 2004 and debuted in 2005. Under Christian Horner and with Adrian Newey's designs it won four double titles with Sebastian Vettel (2010–2013), then dominated the ground-effect era with Max Verstappen. Horner was released in July 2025 and replaced by Laurent Mekies, and the team runs its own Red Bull Ford power unit from 2026.
highlights: Four consecutive double championships with Sebastian Vettel, 2010–2013
Max Verstappen's four straight Drivers' titles, 2021–2024
RB19 won 21 of 22 races in 2023, including a then-record 15 consecutive team wins
Six Constructors' and eight Drivers' Championships

Ferrari.name: Ferrari
Ferrari.history: Founded by Enzo Ferrari in 1929 as a racing outfit for Alfa Romeo, Scuderia Ferrari entered the inaugural 1950 World Championship as a constructor and has raced in every season since. Its golden eras include the Lauda years of the 1970s and the Schumacher–Todt–Brawn dynasty of 1999–2004, and it remains the oldest and most successful team in Formula One.
highlights: Only team to have competed in every World Championship season since 1950
Record 16 Constructors' and 15 Drivers' Championships
Michael Schumacher won five consecutive Drivers' titles (2000–2004) and 72 Grands Prix for the team
Six consecutive Constructors' titles, 1999–2004
Reached its 1,000th Grand Prix at the 2020 Tuscan GP

Williams.name: Williams
Williams.first_entry: 1977 Spanish Grand Prix (as a team; 1978 Argentine GP as a constructor)
Williams.stats_basis: Williams constructor record, 1978–2025 (excludes 1977 season run with a customer March chassis)
Williams.history: Frank Williams and Patrick Head founded Williams Grand Prix Engineering in 1977, building their own cars from 1978 and winning for the first time at the 1979 British GP. With Honda and Renault engines and designers including Head and Adrian Newey, Williams dominated much of the 1980s and 1990s. The family sold the team to Dorilton Capital in 2020, and James Vowles has led its rebuild since 2023.
highlights: Nine Constructors' Championships, a record until Ferrari's tenth in 2000
Seven Drivers' champions: Jones, Rosberg, Piquet, Mansell, Prost, Hill and Villeneuve
Nigel Mansell won a then-record nine races in 1992
Reached 100 Grand Prix wins at the 1997 British GP

Racing Bulls.name: Racing Bulls
Racing Bulls.entry: Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team
Racing Bulls.founder: Red Bull (Dietrich Mateschitz), via purchase of Minardi
Racing Bulls.stats_basis: Combined Toro Rosso (2006–2019), AlphaTauri (2020–2023), RB (2024) and Racing Bulls (2025) record; excludes Minardi (1985–2005)
Racing Bulls.history: The Faenza team began as Minardi, founded by Giancarlo Minardi and in Formula One from 1985 to 2005. Red Bull bought it in 2005 and ran it as Scuderia Toro Rosso from 2006, as AlphaTauri from 2020 to 2023, as RB in 2024 and as Racing Bulls since 2025. It has long served as Red Bull's junior team, bringing through Vettel, Verstappen, Ricciardo, Sainz and Gasly.
highlights: Sebastian Vettel won the 2008 Italian GP from pole, the team's first win and pole
Pierre Gasly won the 2020 Italian GP for AlphaTauri
Isack Hadjar finished third at the 2025 Dutch GP, the first podium under the Racing Bulls name
Feeder team for future world champions Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen

Aston Martin.name: Aston Martin
Aston Martin.founder: Lawrence Stroll (consortium that bought Force India in 2018)
Aston Martin.stats_basis: Aston Martin constructor record, 2021–2025 (excludes 1959–1960 Aston Martin entries and the Jordan/Midland/Spyker/Force India/Racing Point predecessors)
Aston Martin.history: The Silverstone team began as Jordan Grand Prix in 1991 and then raced as Midland (2006), Spyker (2007), Force India (2008–2018) and Racing Point (2019–2020) after Lawrence Stroll's consortium bought it in 2018. It was renamed Aston Martin in 2021, reviving the marque's brief 1959–60 F1 effort. Since then it has built a new factory and wind tunnel, hired Adrian Newey (who became team principal for 2026), and in 2026 became Honda's works team.
highlights: Fernando Alonso scored eight podiums in 2023, the team's best season
Sebastian Vettel finished second at the 2021 Azerbaijan GP, its first podium
Became Honda's works partner from 2026
Lineage wins include Jordan's four victories and Racing Point's 2020 Sakhir GP

Haas F1 Team.name: Haas
Haas F1 Team.base: Kannapolis, United States & Banbury, United Kingdom
Haas F1 Team.history: NASCAR team owner Gene Haas founded Haas F1 in 2014 and debuted in 2016 with a close technical partnership with Ferrari, scoring points in its first race. Guenther Steiner led the team until January 2024, when Ayao Komatsu took over. Toyota Gazoo Racing became its title partner for 2026.
highlights: Scored points on debut at the 2016 Australian GP (Grosjean sixth)
Best Constructors' finish of fifth in 2018
Kevin Magnussen took the team's first pole at the 2022 São Paulo GP
Best race finish of fourth, including Oliver Bearman at the 2025 Mexico City GP

Audi.name: Audi
Audi.stats_basis: Hinwil team record 1993–2025: Sauber, BMW Sauber (2006–2010), Alfa Romeo (2019–2023) and Kick Sauber (2024–2025); Audi constructor began in 2026
Audi.history: Peter Sauber founded the Hinwil company in 1970, won Le Mans and two world sportscar titles, and entered F1 in 1993. BMW owned the team from 2006 to 2009, when it won the 2008 Canadian GP. It then raced under the Sauber, Alfa Romeo and Kick Sauber names before Audi took it over completely, and it became Audi's factory team for 2026.
highlights: Robert Kubica led a BMW Sauber 1–2 at the 2008 Canadian GP, the team's only win
Kubica took the team's only pole at the 2008 Bahrain GP
Nico Hülkenberg finished third at the 2025 British GP, his first podium after 239 starts and the team's first since 2012
Audi's first works F1 team, with its own power unit from 2026

Alpine.name: Alpine
Alpine.principal: Flavio Briatore (executive advisor, de facto team boss)
Alpine.founder: Renault Group (rebrand of Renault F1 Team)
Alpine.history: The Enstone team began as Toleman in 1981, became Benetton in 1986 (titles in 1994–95 with Michael Schumacher), then Renault (titles in 2005–06 with Fernando Alonso), Lotus (2012–2015) and Renault again before being renamed Alpine in 2021. Renault ended its F1 engine programme after 2025, so Alpine has used Mercedes power units since 2026.
highlights: Esteban Ocon won the 2021 Hungarian GP, the team's only win as Alpine
Fernando Alonso finished third at the 2021 Qatar GP
Ocon and Gasly finished second and third at the 2024 São Paulo GP
Lineage includes Benetton's 1995 and Renault's 2005–06 Constructors' titles

Cadillac.name: Cadillac
Cadillac.base: Fishers, Indiana, United States & Silverstone, United Kingdom
Cadillac.stats_basis: New constructor for 2026, so no races before the 2026 season
Cadillac.history: The project began as a joint General Motors and Andretti bid that Formula One initially rejected. After TWG Global took over business operations in late 2024, the entry was approved in March 2025, making Cadillac the grid's 11th team for 2026. It has bases in Silverstone and the United States and uses Ferrari power units until GM's own engine is ready.
highlights: First new team on the grid since Haas in 2016
The grid's 11th team, debuting in 2026 with Sergio Pérez and Valtteri Bottas
Backed by General Motors, with a GM power unit planned for later in the decade
Graeme Lowdon was its first team principal; Marcin Budkowski replaced him in August 2026

2019.sum: Mercedes won a sixth straight double, with Hamilton taking 11 wins and his sixth title, clinched in Austin. Ferrari had the most powerful car on the straights and Charles Leclerc won at Spa and Monza in his first year with the team, while Verstappen gave Honda its first win of the hybrid era in Austria.
keys: Hamilton's sixth drivers' title.
Leclerc won Ferrari's first Monza race since 2010.
Gasly and Kvyat took podiums for Toro Rosso.

2018.sum: Vettel and Ferrari led the early part of the season, but a crash from the lead at Hockenheim and a run of errors let Hamilton pull clear. Hamilton won 11 races and sealed his fifth title in Mexico.
keys: The halo cockpit protection was introduced.
Räikkönen won in Austin, his first win since 2013.
Fernando Alonso left F1 at the end of the season.

2017.sum: New wider cars with more downforce brought Ferrari back into contention, and Vettel led the championship until Singapore, where both Ferraris crashed at the start. Hamilton won five of the next six races and took his fourth title.
keys: Liberty Media's first season in charge of F1.
Hamilton passed Michael Schumacher's record for pole positions.
Mercedes won a fourth straight constructors' title.

2016.sum: Rosberg won the first four races and held off Hamilton in a season-long Mercedes fight, taking the title by five points in Abu Dhabi. He announced his retirement five days later.
keys: Verstappen won the Spanish GP on his Red Bull debut, aged 18, the youngest winner in F1 history.
Mercedes won 19 of 21 races.
Haas joined the grid and scored points on debut.

2015.sum: Mercedes won 16 of 19 races. Hamilton took ten wins and wrapped up his third title with three races left at the United States GP, while Vettel won three races in his first year with Ferrari.
keys: Max Verstappen made his debut at 17.
McLaren's reunion with Honda brought only 27 points.
Rosberg won the last three races of the year.

2014.sum: The 1.6-litre V6 turbo hybrid engines arrived and Mercedes dominated, winning 16 of 19 races. Hamilton and Rosberg fought all year, with Hamilton taking his second title at the double-points finale in Abu Dhabi.
keys: First year of the turbo hybrid power units.
Ricciardo won three races for Red Bull in his first season with the team.
Jules Bianchi was gravely injured at Suzuka.

2013.sum: Vettel won 13 races, including nine in a row to end the season, and took his fourth straight title. Red Bull completed four consecutive doubles in the last year of the V8 engines.
keys: Last season of the 2.4-litre V8 engines.
Hamilton won in Hungary in his first season at Mercedes.
Mark Webber retired at the end of the year.

2012.sum: Seven different drivers won the first seven races. Alonso led for much of the year in a Ferrari that was not the fastest car, but Vettel won four in a row in the autumn and took the title by three points in a wet Brazilian finale.
keys: Eight different race winners.
Kimi Räikkönen won in Abu Dhabi on his return with Lotus.
Vettel became the youngest triple world champion.

2011.sum: Vettel and Red Bull dominated, with 11 wins and a record 15 poles. He clinched his second title with four races to spare in Japan.
keys: DRS and Pirelli tyres arrived, along with the return of KERS.
Button won a rain-hit Canadian GP from last place after six pit stops.
Red Bull's second straight constructors' title.

2010.sum: Four drivers arrived at the final round in Abu Dhabi with a chance of the title. Vettel won the race and the championship, leading the standings for the first time only after the last race, to become the youngest world champion.
keys: Points system changed to 25-18-15.
Refuelling during races was banned.
Michael Schumacher returned with Mercedes; Red Bull won its first constructors' title.

2000.sum: Michael Schumacher won nine races and ended Ferrari's 21-year wait for a drivers' champion, beating Mika Häkkinen after a season-long duel with McLaren. He sealed the title at Suzuka with a race to spare.
keys: Ferrari's first drivers' title since Jody Scheckter in 1979, and Schumacher's third world title.
McLaren lost 10 constructors' points at the Austrian Grand Prix over a missing seal on Häkkinen's car.
Jaguar replaced Stewart on the grid; Jenson Button made his debut with Williams.

2001.sum: Schumacher dominated, winning nine races and clinching the title in Hungary with four rounds to go. Häkkinen won twice in his final season before a sabbatical that became retirement.
keys: Schumacher passed Alain Prost's record of 51 Grand Prix wins.
Kimi Räikkönen, Fernando Alonso and Juan Pablo Montoya made their debuts.
Traction control was allowed again from the Spanish Grand Prix.

2002.sum: Schumacher finished on the podium in every race, won 11 times and clinched the title in France in July, the earliest ever. Ferrari won 15 of the 17 races.
keys: Ferrari's team orders in Austria, where Barrichello handed Schumacher the win, led to a ban on team orders.
Toyota joined the grid and Benetton was renamed Renault.
Arrows ran out of money and left after the German Grand Prix.

2003.sum: The closest title fight in years. A new points system kept Räikkönen in contention until the final race at Suzuka, where Schumacher took eighth place and a record sixth title by two points.
keys: Points were now awarded to the top eight: 10-8-6-5-4-3-2-1.
Fernando Alonso became the youngest Grand Prix winner at the time, in Hungary.
Single-lap qualifying and parc fermé between qualifying and the race were introduced.

2004.sum: Schumacher won 13 of the 18 races, including 12 of the first 13, for his seventh and final world title. His Ferrari team-mate Rubens Barrichello was runner-up.
keys: Schumacher's 13 wins set a new record for a season.
Jenson Button and BAR finished second in the constructors' championship.
Bahrain and China hosted their first Grands Prix.

2005.sum: Fernando Alonso and Renault ended Ferrari's five-year run. Alonso became the youngest world champion at 24, holding off McLaren's Kimi Räikkönen, who won seven races.
keys: Tyre changes during races were banned for the season.
Only six cars started the United States Grand Prix after the Michelin-shod teams withdrew.
Red Bull Racing replaced Jaguar on the grid.

2006.sum: Alonso and Renault beat Michael Schumacher and Ferrari again. The title was settled at the final race in Brazil, Schumacher's last before his first retirement.
keys: 2.4-litre V8 engines replaced the V10s.
Three-part knock-out qualifying was introduced.
Honda, BMW Sauber, Toro Rosso, Midland and Super Aguri joined the grid.

2007.sum: Kimi Räikkönen came from 17 points behind with two races to go to beat McLaren's Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso by a single point.
keys: McLaren was excluded from the constructors' championship and fined 00 million over the espionage case.
Lewis Hamilton finished on the podium in each of his first nine races.
Bridgestone became the sole tyre supplier.

2008.sum: Lewis Hamilton won the title by one point from Felipe Massa, passing Timo Glock in the closing corners of the final race in Brazil to take the fifth place he needed.
keys: Hamilton became the youngest world champion at the time, aged 23.
Singapore hosted the first night race; Sebastian Vettel gave Toro Rosso its first win, at Monza.
A standard electronic control unit ended traction control.

2009.sum: Brawn GP, rescued from Honda's withdrawal, won six of the first seven races with Jenson Button and took both titles in its only season.
keys: New aerodynamic rules, slick tyres and KERS shook up the order.
Double diffusers gave Brawn, Toyota and Williams an early-season advantage.
Red Bull won its first Grand Prix, in China, with Sebastian Vettel.

1950.sum: The first Formula 1 World Championship. Alfa Romeo won every race it entered, and Nino Farina took the title by three points from his team-mate Juan Manuel Fangio.
keys: The championship began at Silverstone on 13 May 1950.
The Indianapolis 500 counted towards the championship from 1950 to 1960, though few regular drivers took part.
Points went to the top five finishers, plus one for the fastest lap.

1951.sum: Juan Manuel Fangio won the first of his five titles for Alfa Romeo, holding off Ferrari's Alberto Ascari at the final race in Spain.
keys: José Froilán González gave Ferrari its first championship win, at Silverstone.
It was Alfa Romeo's last season before withdrawing from Grand Prix racing.

1952.sum: With the championship run to Formula 2 rules, Alberto Ascari won six races in a row for Ferrari and took the title by 12 points.
keys: Formula 2 regulations were used in 1952 and 1953, after Alfa Romeo's withdrawal left too few Formula 1 cars.
Fangio missed the season after breaking his neck in a non-championship race at Monza.

1953.sum: Ascari retained the title for Ferrari with five wins, ahead of Fangio, now driving for Maserati.
keys: Ascari's run of nine consecutive championship wins, from Belgium 1952 to Belgium 1953, stood as the record for 70 years.
Mike Hawthorn beat Fangio by a second at Reims to become the first British driver to win a championship Grand Prix.

1954.sum: Fangio won his second title. He started the season with Maserati, then moved to the returning Mercedes-Benz team and won on its debut at Reims.
keys: Mercedes returned with the W196, raced with streamlined bodywork at fast circuits.
New 2.5-litre engine rules began.

1955.sum: Fangio and Mercedes dominated again, with Stirling Moss second in the sister car. Moss won the British Grand Prix at Aintree, his first championship win.
keys: After the Le Mans disaster in June several races were cancelled, and Switzerland banned motor racing.
Alberto Ascari was killed testing a sports car at Monza.
Mercedes withdrew from racing at the end of the season.

1956.sum: Fangio won a fourth title, for Ferrari, after Peter Collins handed over his car at the final race at Monza, giving up his own chance of the championship.
keys: Stirling Moss joined Maserati and won at Monaco and Monza.

1957.sum: Fangio won his fifth and final title, for Maserati, including his famous comeback drive at the Nürburgring to win the German Grand Prix.
keys: Moss and Tony Brooks won the British Grand Prix in a shared Vanwall, the first championship win for a British car.
Fangio's five titles stood as the record until 2003.

1958.sum: Mike Hawthorn became the first British world champion, by a single point from Stirling Moss, despite winning only one race.
keys: The constructors' championship was awarded for the first time, to Vanwall.
Moss spoke up for Hawthorn when he faced disqualification in Portugal, which proved decisive.
Peter Collins and Stuart Lewis-Evans were killed during the season.

1959.sum: Jack Brabham won the title in a rear-engined Cooper, pushing his car over the line at the final race at Sebring.
keys: Cooper won the constructors' title, beginning the end of front-engined Grand Prix cars.
Bruce McLaren became the youngest Grand Prix winner at the time, at Sebring.

1960.sum: Brabham and Cooper retained both titles, with Brabham winning five races in a row in the middle of the season.
keys: It was the last year the Indianapolis 500 counted towards the championship.
Stirling Moss gave Lotus its first championship win, at Monaco, in Rob Walker's privately entered car.

1961.sum: New 1.5-litre engine rules favoured Ferrari's 'sharknose' 156. Phil Hill became the first American world champion after his team-mate Wolfgang von Trips was killed at Monza.
keys: Stirling Moss won at Monaco and the Nürburgring in an older, less powerful Lotus.

1962.sum: Graham Hill won the title for BRM after Jim Clark's Lotus retired from the lead of the final race in South Africa.
keys: The Lotus 25 introduced the monocoque chassis to Formula 1.
Stirling Moss's career ended after a crash at Goodwood in April.

1963.sum: Jim Clark won seven of the ten races for Lotus, a record for a season at the time.
keys: Clark also finished second in the Indianapolis 500.

1964.sum: John Surtees won the title for Ferrari by a single point from Graham Hill at the final race in Mexico, and remains the only world champion on both two and four wheels.
keys: Jim Clark lost the title when his engine failed on the last lap in Mexico.

1965.sum: Jim Clark won his second title with six wins and also won the Indianapolis 500, missing Monaco to race there.
keys: It was the last season of the 1.5-litre formula.
Honda took its first win, with Richie Ginther in Mexico.

1966.sum: Jack Brabham won the first season of the 3-litre formula in a car of his own, the only driver to win the title in a car bearing his name.
keys: Brabham's car used a Repco V8 engine from Australia.

1967.sum: Denny Hulme beat his team boss Jack Brabham to the title, and Brabham-Repco won the constructors' championship again.
keys: The Cosworth DFV won on its debut at Zandvoort, driven by Jim Clark.
Lorenzo Bandini died after a crash at Monaco.

1968.sum: Graham Hill led a grieving Lotus to both titles after Jim Clark was killed in a Formula 2 race at Hockenheim in April.
keys: Wings appeared on Formula 1 cars for the first time.
Lotus raced in Gold Leaf colours, beginning the era of sponsors' liveries.

1969.sum: Jackie Stewart won his first title with six wins in Ken Tyrrell's Matra.
keys: Several teams tried four-wheel drive and abandoned it.

1970.sum: Jochen Rindt became the only posthumous world champion after he was killed in practice at Monza; no one overtook his points total.
keys: Bruce McLaren was killed testing at Goodwood, and Piers Courage at Zandvoort.
The Lotus 72 introduced side-mounted radiators.

1971.sum: Jackie Stewart and Tyrrell dominated, winning six races in the team's first full season with its own car.
keys: Peter Gethin won at Monza by 0.01 seconds, the closest finish at the time.

1972.sum: Emerson Fittipaldi became the youngest world champion at the time, aged 25, in the black-and-gold Lotus 72.
keys: Lotus raced in John Player Special colours.

1973.sum: Jackie Stewart won his third title and retired, missing what would have been his 100th race after his team-mate François Cevert was killed at Watkins Glen.
keys: Lotus won the constructors' championship.

1974.sum: Emerson Fittipaldi won his second title, McLaren's first, after a three-way fight that went to the final race.
keys: McLaren also won its first constructors' championship.

1975.sum: Niki Lauda won the title for Ferrari with five wins, the team's first drivers' championship since 1964.
keys: Half points were awarded in Spain and Austria, where races were stopped early.

1976.sum: James Hunt won the title by one point at the rain-soaked final race in Japan, after Niki Lauda returned only six weeks after his near-fatal crash at the Nürburgring.
keys: Lauda withdrew from the race at Fuji, judging the conditions too dangerous.
Ferrari won the constructors' championship.

1977.sum: Niki Lauda won his second title for Ferrari, then left the team before the season ended.
keys: Renault introduced the turbocharged engine at the British Grand Prix.
Tom Pryce was killed at Kyalami.

1978.sum: Mario Andretti won the title in the ground-effect Lotus 79, with his team-mate Ronnie Peterson second.
keys: Peterson died after a crash at the start of the Italian Grand Prix.
Brabham's 'fan car' won in Sweden and was then withdrawn.

1979.sum: Jody Scheckter won the title for Ferrari, with Gilles Villeneuve second; it was Ferrari's last drivers' title until 2000.
keys: Jean-Pierre Jabouille won the French Grand Prix at Dijon, the first win for a turbocharged car.
Villeneuve and René Arnoux fought wheel to wheel for second place in the same race.

1980.sum: Alan Jones won the first drivers' title for Williams, and the team took the constructors' championship too.
keys: The Spanish Grand Prix lost its championship status during the FISA–FOCA dispute.

1981.sum: Nelson Piquet won the title for Brabham by one point from Carlos Reutemann at the final race in Las Vegas.
keys: The first Concorde Agreement ended the FISA–FOCA war.

1982.sum: Keke Rosberg won the title for Williams with a single victory, in a season with 11 different winners.
keys: Gilles Villeneuve was killed in qualifying at Zolder, and Riccardo Paletti at the start in Canada.
Didier Pironi led the championship until a crash in practice at Hockenheim ended his career.

1983.sum: Nelson Piquet won his second title, the first for a turbocharged car, beating Alain Prost at the final race.
keys: Flat bottoms became compulsory, ending the ground-effect era.

1984.sum: Niki Lauda won his third title by half a point from his McLaren team-mate Alain Prost, the smallest margin in championship history.
keys: McLaren won 12 of the 16 races.
Half points were awarded at the rain-shortened Monaco Grand Prix.

1985.sum: Alain Prost became France's first world champion, winning five races for McLaren.
keys: Ayrton Senna won for the first time, in the rain in Portugal.

1986.sum: Prost retained the title at the final race in Adelaide, where Nigel Mansell's tyre exploded while he was on course for the championship.
keys: Williams won the constructors' championship.
It was the last season of unlimited turbo boost.

1987.sum: Nelson Piquet won his third title for Williams after his team-mate Nigel Mansell was injured in practice in Japan.
keys: Williams-Honda won the constructors' championship.

1988.sum: Ayrton Senna won his first title as McLaren won 15 of the 16 races.
keys: Prost scored more points overall, but only each driver's best 11 results counted.
It was the last season of turbocharged engines until 2014.

1989.sum: Alain Prost won his third title after colliding with his team-mate Ayrton Senna at the chicane at Suzuka; Senna was disqualified from the race.
keys: Turbo engines were banned in favour of 3.5-litre engines.

1990.sum: Ayrton Senna won his second title after colliding with Prost, now at Ferrari, at the first corner at Suzuka.
keys: McLaren won the constructors' championship for the third year running.

1991.sum: Senna won his third title for McLaren, winning the first four races.
keys: Michael Schumacher made his debut for Jordan at Spa.

1992.sum: Nigel Mansell won the title with nine wins in the dominant, active-suspension Williams FW14B, clinching it in Hungary in August.
keys: Michael Schumacher won his first race, at Spa.

1993.sum: Alain Prost won his fourth title for Williams and retired at the end of the season.
keys: Ayrton Senna won five races for McLaren, including the European Grand Prix at Donington.
It was the last year of active suspension and traction control.

1994.sum: Michael Schumacher won his first title, by one point from Damon Hill, after the two collided at the final race in Adelaide.
keys: Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger were killed at Imola.
Schumacher was disqualified twice and banned for two races.

1995.sum: Schumacher retained the title with nine wins and gave Benetton its only constructors' championship.
keys: Engines were reduced to 3 litres.

1996.sum: Damon Hill won the title for Williams, the first son of a world champion to win it, ahead of his team-mate Jacques Villeneuve.
keys: Michael Schumacher joined Ferrari and won three races.

1997.sum: Jacques Villeneuve won the title for Williams at the final race at Jerez, where Michael Schumacher drove into him and was later excluded from the championship.
keys: Schumacher's race results stand, but he is listed as excluded from the drivers' standings.

1998.sum: Mika Häkkinen won his first title for McLaren after a season-long fight with Michael Schumacher.
keys: Narrower cars and grooved tyres were introduced.

1999.sum: Häkkinen retained the title by two points from Ferrari's Eddie Irvine, who led Ferrari's challenge after Michael Schumacher broke his leg at Silverstone.
keys: Ferrari won its first constructors' title since 1983.

PREWAR.sum: Grand Prix racing restarted in 1946, but the Formula 1 World Championship only began in 1950. From 1946 to 1949 there were no points and no champion: every race stood on its own. The most prestigious races were named Grandes Épreuves by the FIA.
keys: The new Formula A, soon called Formula One, allowed 1.5-litre supercharged or 4.5-litre unsupercharged engines. It became the official formula on 1 January 1947, though some races still used other rules.
Alfa Romeo, Maserati, Talbot-Lago, ERA and later Ferrari built most of the winning cars.
The first World Championship round was the British Grand Prix at Silverstone on 13 May 1950.

1946.sum: The first season after the Second World War. There was no championship and no race counted as a Grande Épreuve. Raymond Sommer was the most successful driver with five wins (one shared), and Maserati won half of the races.
keys: The Turin Grand Prix in September was the first race run to the new Formula A (Formula One) rules.
Alfa Romeo won six races, including Turin and Milan, and the Grand Prix des Nations in Geneva.

1947.sum: The first full season of Formula One rules. The Swiss, Belgian, Italian and French Grands Prix were the Grandes Épreuves. Alfa Romeo won three of them and 13 races in all; Luigi Villoresi won six races, more than anyone else.
keys: Jean-Pierre Wimille won the Swiss and Belgian Grands Prix for Alfa Romeo.
Louis Chiron won the French Grand Prix at Lyon-Parilly for Talbot-Lago.
The season began in South America, with races in Brazil and Argentina.

1948.sum: Maserati won 13 of the 23 races here, and Luigi Villoresi was the top winner again with six. The four Grandes Épreuves were Monaco, Switzerland, France and Italy: Wimille won two for Alfa Romeo, Farina won Monaco for Maserati and Trossi won in Switzerland.
keys: Achille Varzi was killed in practice for the Swiss Grand Prix at Bremgarten.
Silverstone held its first British Grand Prix, won by Villoresi.
Nino Farina won the Circuito del Garda in a Ferrari.

1949.sum: The last year before the World Championship. Alfa Romeo stayed away, and Maserati, Ferrari and Talbot-Lago shared the wins. Five races were Grandes Épreuves. Alberto Ascari and Juan Manuel Fangio won five races each.
keys: Jean-Pierre Wimille was killed in practice in Buenos Aires in January.
Fangio's first European season brought wins at San Remo, Pau, Perpignan, Marseille and Albi.
Ascari won the Swiss and Italian Grands Prix for Ferrari.
